segments.text: Starting our first plenary today, and I'll be happy to moderate it. My name is Hala Youssef, and I work as the Sexual Reproductive Health Advisor for UNFPA Arab States Office. We're based in Cairo, and actually, we're starting our discussions today with pillar one from the Global Midwifery Accelerator.

I assume that everyone knows now that the Global Midwifery Accelerator is a unified global partnership led by UNFPA in coalition with WHO, UNICEF, International Confederation of Midwives, JAPAGO, John JAPAGO, and the accelerator is an evidence driven initiative to scale up midwife-led models of care worldwide. Under pillar one, we're looking for strengthening the national policies and regulatory frameworks where we start to jump into the midwifery models of care. So, we need to keep our midwives in the front as leaders, not under any other administration, and the scopes of practice should not prevent them from performing emergency procedures.

The regulatory councils should support them to continue professional development and make resilient health systems that absorb the workforce of midwives. So, actually, we are having distinguished panelists that will join us today from different organizations. We'll start with an overview of how policies emerge.

So, I'm sure everyone in this room has gone through some policy debates around midwives and how does this strengthen their roles in a country, but how do we evolve in that? We have a very good experience with the League of Arab States, which is an intergovernmental body in northern Africa, and it works with all 22 Arab countries in the Arab region on advancing policies that support midwifery, and I want to tell you that this work is always through the Ministerial Health Council, led by ministers from different countries of the region. So, we will go to a very short video that explains this with Ms. Maisa El-Hedmi, who is the Minister of Planned Potentiality and the Director of Health and Humanitarian Division of the Social Sector at the League of Arab States in Cairo, and she has recorded this message to show us the developments that we passed through at regional and national levels. So, can we play the video, please? Ladies and gentlemen, it's a pleasure to address you today on behalf of the League of Arab States, Arab Health Ministers Council, and to highlight our long-standing partnership with the United Nations Population Fund, particularly its Arab States regional office.

Our partnership reflects a shared commitment to strengthening health systems, advancing the health and well-being of women and families, and supporting Arab countries in addressing their health and development priorities. We firmly believe that sustainable progress cannot be achieved through isolated initiatives. It requires strong regional cooperation, national ownership, institutional commitment, and continuous investment in the health workforce.

In this regard, our collaboration with UNFPA has been particularly valuable in supporting regional strategies, facilitating the exchange of expertise, strengthening national capacities, and providing a platform for dialogue among Arab countries. Our focus today is on midwifery, as midwives are at the heart of maternal and newborn health. They deliver quality care to women, expand access to reproductive health services, and ensure continuity of care, especially in vulnerable communities.

Investing in midwifery is one of the most effective ways to save lives and strengthen health systems in developing countries. This is why we regard the Arab strategy for nursing and midwifery as a significant regional milestone, and one of the most important areas of this cooperation. Its real value lies in helping member states turn regional priorities into practical national actions.

It gives each country a shared framework to assess its situation, identify gaps, and build its own plans according to its needs and capacities. Arab countries differ in their development levels and workforce challenges. Therefore, the implementation of these strategies must remain nationally driven.

For example, Egypt has developed its strategy in line with its national priorities, while Jordan and Morocco have begun developing and exploring legal frameworks to support midwives. Our main aim is to help countries strengthen midwifery education, improve workforce planning and distribution, enhance regulation and leadership, and create an enabling environment where midwives can practice to the full scope of their competencies. Technical support is essential in this matter.

Our collaboration with UNFPA mobilizes expertise, supports national assessments, and helps countries find the right approaches of implementation. Our joint workshops are practical platforms for listening to countries and understanding their realities, workforce shortages, and training needs to professional regulation, career development, and retention. Looking ahead, the next phase should focus on accelerating implementation through stronger national action plans, structured technical assistance, regular regional workshops, and clear indicators to measure progress.

Documentation of successful national experiences can help countries lead from one each other. We are ambitious to move from a regional strategy to tangible results in every member state, a stronger midwifery profession, better prepared professionals, more resilient health systems, and healthier mothers and newborns. I would like to express our sincere appreciation to UNFPA and its Arab States Regional Office for their continued partnership and technical support.

We look forward to further strengthening this collaboration and working together with all Arab countries to turn our shared vision into concrete and sustainable results. Thank you. Well, I want also to thank the League of Arab States for their commitment and their support to midwifery policies and setting strategies at regional and national levels.

But this is only the beginning, the commitment. So a policy is a commitment from the country to provide the necessary support, and it differs from country to country. And we need to know more about the whole of Africa.

So may I invite our distinguished panelists who are going to walk us through the different workforce needs and the regulatory approaches in different countries of the region. First, we have Dr. Eba Seka, the Senior Technical Officer for Maternal Reproductive Health in CDC Africa. Please have a seat.

And I call also on our second speaker, who is Dr. Christiana Mansalai, the Registrar of the National Nursing and Midwifery Council in Sierra Leone. Can you join our stage, please? And I join my sweet UNFA colleagues from different regions in Africa, Dr. Mona Abdalla from Eastern Southern Africa. She is the Sexual Reproductive Health Advisor.
I invite Hilma Shikawambi, from West Africa. And finally, my colleague, Mwali Fair, the Regional SRH Specialist in the UNFPA Arab States. Welcome to this panel.

Actually, I think as we move, we will get more insights from the whole of Africa. And we start with Dr. Eba Seka, who is going to speak about the state of health workforce in Africa and give us more insight to what are the needs, what's the situation. Inform us, please.
Dr. Eba, you have the floor. Yes, thank you. Can we play the presentation? Okay.
Yeah, thank you very much. Yeah, I bring you greetings from the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. My name is Eba.

I'm a Senior Technical Officer working under the RAMCA division under the Centers for Primary Health Care. And the Director of Primary Health Care, Dr. Landry, he regrets, apologizes for not being able to be physically here. And Dr. Diana, who is also very passionate as far as this subject is concerned, you all know about it.

Just to start with, I want to remind you that in 2006, the special session of the African Union Health Ministers adopted the Mabutu Plan of Action. And the goal was for all stakeholders and partners to join forces to enable effective implementation of the policy framework. And you will agree with me that further down, as far as policies are concerned, the Mabutu Plan of Action 2016-2030 was subsequently endorsed in Kigali here, that was on the 27th of the AU Summit in 2016.

So based on this, the continental framework and policies, the African CDC, they felt, developed a five-year reproductive health priorities to support the implementation of the Mabutu Plan of Action. My issue is like, I have many slides. The clicker is not working.
I'm not getting... Okay. This is just a global perspective, looking into indicators, which many speakers have talked about. I'll spend less time on that.

But most importantly, 69% of the global maternal deaths are in Africa. And the complications that are leading those mothers to dying, 75% of the maternal deaths are due to severe hemorrhage, infection, high blood pressure, in which the midwives are very critical in managing. It's the complications that are killing the mothers.

The midwives need the skills, you understand, to manage those complications. Further down my presentation, you came to realize that African CDC developed a five-year reproductive health priorities, and it has a mission, a vision, and a goal. It wants to ensure a safer, healthier, integrated, and responsive prosperous Africa.

And the mission was to strengthen African public health institutions' capacities and capabilities, and also partnership. The goal ultimately was to reduce maternal mortality, which is an impact indicator in which the old sectors must have to come on board. One single institution cannot do it.

So further down, if you look at it, we were guided by seven broad objectives as far as the priority strategy is concerned, which expands from 2022 to 2026. It should be ending this year. So we were thinking of ways of evaluating it.

So the objectives broadly look into the collaboration, increased capacity, support member states, and ensuring also the supplies of reproductive health commodities, which is very critical, especially the heat-stable capitals, you understand, and other, you know, reproductive health commodities that help in saving the lives of the women are concerned are available. Further down, we want to also support member states to expand, you understand, the workforce, in which the midwifery workforce is very critical in this aspect. And we need more midwives.

The Director General of African CDC just stated this morning about the relevance of getting the required human resource as far as the midwifery workforce is concerned, available in saving the lives of the women. Ensuring also there is that contribution when it comes to the resources, when it comes to the money that you put on the table. The evidence told us the few countries in Africa meet the Abuja Declaration, when we're talking about 10 of the 15 percent of the national budget to get into resolve.

So we want to also improve the RH manager's capacity. And the online priority survey that the African CDC did, that informed the policy, showed that there are gaps around that area. Skills, the gaps around skills to make sure that the accountability is in place.

Gaps around the area, some leadership. So in my presentation for you, that necessitated for African CDC to bring 14 African Union member states to train them on leadership, to give them some leadership skills. The clicker is okay.

Now, when we did that online priority survey that informed the strategy, the African CDC strategy to help reduce maternal mortality, you know, six fundamental elements were prioritized by member states. Remember, 42 African Union member states convicted at Addis Ababa that recommended that adolescent and sexual and reproductive health services should be prioritized. And you will agree with me that, you understand, that over 70 percent of the population in Africa are the youth, and we need to break that demographic dividend.

And this is very important. Maternal and newborn service and family planning, prevention and control of RH reproductive health cancer. They are the silent killers, you understand, gender-based violence, safe abortion care.

And member states felt that for this to happen, there must be some effective communication between people. So interpersonal communication came in. But this way I aligned to three main building blocks as far as work is concerned.
The health financing, health work, the workforce development, and leadership and governance. I have many slides. Because of time, I am going to limit myself.

I have about five minutes. One fundamental thing that we realized was there was need to give the skills to the frontline money, which the midwives is critical. African CDC developed the curriculum to train midwives on emergency obstetric care services.
And this we did together in partnership with Liverpool's Public Commission. I am recognizing some of the midwives present here who we trained ourselves. We got continental team of trainers.
We felt member states should be empowered. So we bought the equipments. We got a continental team of trainers to go down to train.
This is the space that UNFPA have been doing for so long. So we came in a different way in our presence. So if you look at the pictures here, that's it.

The online priority survey that informed also this document indicated that there were policy gaps. So we did a quick assessment of the policies. You understand? So two key countries where you need to be supported.
I could recognize some people here that we work with. The Republic of Cameroon was one of it. And Lesotho.
We supported them to develop five-year reproductive health strategy. The policies need to be there. Whatever we did, evidence should be evidence-based.
It's the evidence that should dictate the practice. So that was very, very important. If you look at it, I think you can see Dr. Ibongo present here and also some people that we supported.
These are live pictures that are showing the support that we get. We plan with countries. We support them over time to develop these policies.
One minute, sir. One minute, yes, just to come. One very important thing that led to the champions as far as Tanzania is concerned, we did a leadership training for 14 African Union member states.

Out of that, Tanzania did a presentation and indicated that they were able to reduce maternal mortality by 80% within a span of six, seven years. We felt there was a reason behind the numbers. African CDC mobilized about 14 African Union member states and we traveled to Tanzania for a continental study talk.
So we came to realize that there were reasons also for the number. That's it over there. We came to realize that key things came out of that support.

Facilitate knowledge. Can you please go back to the other slide just quickly, please? I know I have little time. The political commitment, the workforce expansion, the health infrastructure development, the capacity building, and the robust will were key of the things.

There was the political commitment, which is very important. There was also maternal and perinatal death reviews instituted, which was also included. The community health system, the referral system, as far as the MMA was concerned, was another thing.

Those were all good practices in the land, leading to the champion now of Her Excellency Samuel Nsuru as the champion of maternal death. The African CDC is committed to move this agenda. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Dr. Eba for this very comprehensive presentation. And this is what we wish would happen. This is what we're looking for.

So the workforce, but then for implementation, we have to cross one river in the middle, and this is the regulations. So regulatory procedures help in supporting midwifery models of care, relicensing, other issues that Dr. Christiana would speak about and help us understand what do we need to do more. Over to you, Dr. Casteel.
If you wish to come here, please. The flicker. This way? This way? So the slide, please.
Okay. You look at this side. Yeah, so it's working.
Good afternoon, colleagues. So I bring you greetings from the Sierra Leone Seminary Council members. Of course, the chairperson is here.
So we became a council in 2023. That elevates us from board to council. And so previously, we were over this on my left hand.

But now, after the 2023 Acts of Parliament, we have autonomy as a council. The governance is full regulatory autonomy, funding, independent source allocation, and modernized legislative authority. We do not have to obtain permission if we want to make, to improve, to bring on board new standards, SOPs.

We do it ourselves because we have the autonomy. When we evolve as the health, the midwifery sector evolves because we are not working in silos. So with the council, we are working with three pillars.

One is independence regulation, resource allocation, and statutory independence. All of them, you can find out the autonomy of our set of training standards as I have just told you. When we are bored, we have to obtain permission from everybody.

We need to do this. How do we go about it? But now that we are a council, we have the autonomy to do exactly as other councils that we have gone to share experience from, to learn from, have told us. And we are working on the financial operation control and the self-governance council autonomy under law.

We make our own laws as midwives. We make our own laws now that we think will benefit the midwifery institutions, the subjects, the staff, the institution, and the subjects. We do all this so that midwifery will be applicable, quality service delivery, and respectful maternal care is being rendered to all of our pregnant women that attend our clinics.
So our workforce evolution, modern practice, and new cadres. With midwifery now, in the past, before you do midwifery, midwifery used to be a post-basic program. We implemented it.
We would have done nothing before you become a midwife, either an RN or state-enrolled community health nurse. But we have changed that trajectory. We now take direct from school.
Yes, so many things led to that. Our midwives were dying. We did not have enough of them.
The experience was little. So now we've changed that. We now take direct from school.

That is a modernized something that we brought on board. And recently, as we said last week, we've got our first cohorts of direct entry into midwifery. And they are now ready to be sent on internship.

And after the internship, they will come back, and they will be licensed and start to work. Midwifery recognition, we incorporate advanced midwifery specialists. Our career pathway has now gone as far as PhD in midwifery.

We've gone all out, that if you do your direct entry into midwifery, it's your diploma, or you start with BSc in nursing, masters in nursing, you work and you can be a PhD. We've made all those available now, so that midwifery will be recognized in Sierra Leone. And we are not doing this in silos.
We are producing for Ministry of Health. So whatever we do, it aligns with what they have. So one of the documents that we are proud of in Sierra Leone is the scope of practice and standards.

We never had one, but with the help of our development partners, we've developed one, and we have distributed it to all the training institutions that we have, and also the midwifery, maternity wards, wherever midwifery is being done, we've distributed those standards, those books to them. And this autonomous scope of practice, defines clear ethnical boundaries across all cadres. For instance, if I'm a midwife, what am I supposed to do? Where will be my stopping point? And a best midwife is a midwife who operates within her scope.
I can't do this, so I'm going to refer. So we are doing monitoring to make sure that our midwives adhere to their scope of practice. One minute, Dr. Christina.
National norms and standards. We establish uniform measurements for safe patient care. We start with the curriculum.

Whatever is being taught in one institution is the same all over the four institutions. And whatever training that we bring on board should be the same for all the midwives, so that you can't be immature and say, okay, because I'm immature, I will not operate as those that are in faculty of nursing in Freetown. So you adhere to what you are supposed to do.
So we are growing in Sierra Leone. We are really growing. So professional advancement, we are now on digital and ethical, we do digital and ethical oversight.
We visit, we look at what you are doing, or you tell us. There's a communication between the regulatory body and the institutions. We sit in our office and know what they are doing.
The career pathway, as I've told you, is structured. We are happy to have UNFPA, they've funded a digital platform for us. And that platform is helping the regulatory body in Sierra Leone.

So UNFPA, on behalf of the council, I want everybody to know that our digital platform that is all over the world, as we entered Malawi the last time, they said, oh, Sierra Leone is a midwifery council. We have seen your digital platform, it is working. So that was funded by UNFPA, through our visionary minister, and it was developed by DSTI.

So that's why we are working on it. We want the practicing nurses, midwives, nurses and midwives to register on it, so that we can do our registrations, our CPDs, our licensing and verification. So CPD framework mandatory, learning for license renewal.
In Sierra Leone now, you work for two years, our license, every two years, we renew our license. You cannot just come, I have come to renew, no, no, no. You have to do CPD points.
And we are starting with 20, 20 new CPD points. You bring it, now we renew your license. If you do not bring them, your license will not be renewed.
Okay, finished. Thank you very much. That was really a great example of one country who passed through the details of regulation in front of us.

So we all know what are the steps, what should we look for. Actually, progress in different countries of the UNFPA, different regions across Africa, is not uniform. Some countries have enacted statutory legislation, recognizing midwifery as a distinct profession, and others have draft legislations not yet finished.

We want to learn more from our UNFPA colleagues in the different regions, and may I call Dr. Mona Abdallah, the regional SRHR advisor at UNFPA Eastern Southern Africa, to give us the idea about this region. Thank you so much, Hala, and good afternoon, everyone. So quickly, this is data generated in 2024 around a state of midwifery in the Eastern Southern Africa region, focusing on policy and regulation.

As it's been said, there has been really a lot of progress in our region. Out of the 23 countries, 14 countries legally recognized midwifery as distinct from nursing, but it also shows the gap that we have a long way to go. Before the midwifery model of care position paper was issued, this is 2024.

Encouragingly, there were 10 countries who have been really implementing some form of midwifery-related care. By then, all countries have a licensing system. However, looking at relicensing, the requirement of CPD for relicensing, we still have 15 countries lagging behind.

We looked at also brain drain, which was commonly known for doctors, but really coming to the midwifery and the mid-level health workers, and we looked at countries who have recognized it as a problem and who put in place strategies. We looked at scope of practices. 19 countries have still missing one or two essential interventions from the scope of practice.

My next slide will focus on what are these tracer interventions. As it has been said, also midwives can provide more than 90% of sexual and productive health services, but these are tracer interventions. 15 tracers are selected on the seven basic EMOC signal function.

Now, they are expanded. The contraceptives and others, particularly on post-abortion care and medical abortion, if the midwives are authorized to provide these services. As you can see, we are doing very well.

Many countries have really improved on the scope of practice, although there is also implementation gap, but you could see that when it comes to medical abortion, certain countries still do not allow midwives to provide this medical abortion, especially in connection with adolescent and young girls, unintended pregnancy, gaps around assisted vaginal delivery, manual vacuum aspiration. My last slide is around an external factor, which is also related with safeguarding pregnant women as well as midwives. This external factor is a disaster.

We have so many disasters, extreme heat, flood, drought, but we focused on extreme heat. Exposure to extreme heat is really imminent. Many of our countries are talking about not just 40 degrees centigrade, we are reaching 50 degrees centigrade, and the implication it has with all pregnancy, commodity and supplies, health workers' exposure to heat stress.

This is really also compounded with the environment the midwives are working in, including the personal protective they use for delivery and so on, really expose them to heat stress and make them errors, a lot of psychosocial issues, emotional issues, and the need for really caring for the caregivers. Maybe let me just go to the last slide. Let me just stop.

Thank you very much, Mona, for giving us an idea about the region and how external factors can influence the regulations. Helma, will you give us some examples from West Africa? What's the situation there, and how does regulation differ across your countries? What are the efforts of UNFPA? The presentation is a little bit... No, you have to go back. Good afternoon.

While we are getting the slide of the context of Western Central Africa, I just want probably to give a bit of a context of the region. We have 23 countries in our region, of which eight out of those countries are currently classified as in humanitarian settings, and we know that with all the global maternal deaths that have been recorded, we talk about sub-Saharan Africa, but part of that sits in Western Central Africa, and also to know that the majority of this maternal death does happen in humanitarian settings, and as I've said, we have about eight countries in our region that are facing this. About three countries in our region have the highest maternal mortality in the world.

So, while the slide is coming, we did our survey surrounding the same time that Eastern Central and Eastern Southern Africa were doing their studies too, around 2024, and we surveyed around 22 countries. So, I'm not so sure what's happening to the slide, but maybe I can just refer to my own notes. So, out of our surveys, okay, so out of the survey that we did, I'm picking out only on the data on the regulatory environment, and out of the 22 countries that we surveyed, only eight countries have a dedicated midwifery regulatory body.

Out of the same number, we have about only eight countries, Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad, Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, if I can mention Gabon, Guinea, and Niger, who has got a regulatory body specifically for midwifery. Quite a bunch of our countries have no separate regulatory body. There is an existence of a regulatory body in the country, however, it caters for both nursing and midwifery.

Three countries in our region have no separate regulatory body that focuses on midwifery, and at the same time, we have about six countries in our region that have got no regulatory bodies at all for midwifery. We are working through strengthening the development of regulatory, because we have heard from our colleagues, if we do not have a regulation that is actually allowing midwifery to practice as autonomous, we are likely to face the burden of maternal death, and sometimes the data really does show us where to go, and for this platform, we are looking forward to engage more on how we can strengthen the regulatory bodies in the Western Central Africa region. Thank you very much.

Thank you so much, Helma, for this comprehensive update on the regulation in West Africa, and now we come to Molly, who will speak about the Northern Africa, and the floor is yours. Great, thank you so much. Oh, excellent.
Okay, it's the previous one. Should be one back. The previous one.

Okay, yeah, it's fine, and so, again, we took some time in the beginning of the session with the comments from Mesa, our colleague from the League of Arab States, and so, you'll find across North Africa, which we define, we being UNFPA, by our own regional boundaries, let's say, and I know sometimes it varies, so when I mention North Africa, I'm talking about Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, Libya, Egypt, Somalia, Sudan, and Djibouti, so there's eight countries that are members of the League of Arab States that are also, that we count as our countries, our African countries, for our office and in our reporting. Overall, it's a highly uneven regulatory landscape, so again, it's really interesting if you look at history and the way that the countries have advanced, let's say, so where we have a midwifery, which is, I would say, stronger and better embedded in the health system, is Tunisia, Morocco, and Algeria. On the other hand, in Libya and Egypt, it's a struggle, so we hear really positive statements from Egypt, and it's so exciting.
Egypt is the largest country in all of Africa. I'm looking at my Ethiopia. Ethiopia is close with us.

We're one of the largest. Egypt is one of the largest, so it's very exciting that there's commitment to advancing midwifery. However, we have a really long way to go, so both in Libya and in Egypt, you'll find recent progress in terms of regulation, but implementation is challenged.

We have highly medicalized systems, really high out-of-pocket expenditure, and a lot of dependence on the private sector, which, of course, is a bit more difficult to regulate. When it comes to Somalia, Sudan, and Djibouti, the situation is quite different. In those countries where we find maternal mortality rates which are quite high and more similar, I would say, to East and Southern and West and Central Africa, the midwives, we can't deny their presence.

We can't deny that the health system depends on them. However, there's a lot of challenges when it comes to the deployment, the distribution, and the retention of the midwives, often working in very challenging settings with limited resources. So again, if you think about the diversity of our sub-region, the regulatory framework matches it.

One challenge that we have when it comes particularly to scope of practice, if you look at the bottom point, is that of those eight countries, at the time of our regional midwifery survey, which was way back in 2022, only two, Djibouti and Morocco, were countries that allowed for midwives to perform the seven BMOC signal functions. Again, we know they've increased since then, but that's a very telling tale. So even in countries where there are developed scopes of practice, we find extremely limited autonomy.

Again, Dr. Mason mentioned the fact that our strategy in trying to work in North Africa is really to work from the top in many ways and to get the commitment of the ministries to look and to really value midwifery models, whatever shape they can take, and work toward strengthening the profession. And so that's why, again, we're working closely with the League of Arab States, and we see success through that. We've recently launched with the Arab health ministers an Arabic brief, a policy brief, about midwifery models.

What does that mean? How could that apply to the region? And based on that, we're getting some requests now to have updated workforce data, etc. So we see progress, but overall, particularly when I look at our colleagues in West and Central and East and Southern Africa, overall we're lagging. So it's really an opportunity to be here and to hear from your regions and from your countries.
The last slide is just... No, I think it's okay. It's okay, I hand the floor back to Dr. Hallam. Thank you so much, Molly, for this update on our region, the Arab States region.

So actually, what we heard now just opens the floor to the debate we have on a shared consensus. Training midwives alone without legal protection will not help. We need to pass the walk or walk the talk, like WHO colleagues say, so in order to have this legal protection, clinical autonomy, public absorption within the economic and health system challenges we're living.

Actually, I was looking to get commitments today, but it seems we want to finish the session and go to the second session. So I want to thank our panelists, Dr. Eba, Dr. Christiana, Mona, Hilma, and Molly, and just raise one point, parliamentarians are important to be engaged in the process of regulation, because we have mentioned examples from Africa, but there are some countries outside Africa that have problems because of non-parliamentary engagement. So I think this is very important to close with.
Thank you very much, colleagues, and thank you, panelists. Thank you. Now, may I invite Julia Bluestone and Molly Fair, Molly, to brief us on our interactive road map sessions.
Over to you. Great, so thank you. Sorry, we're going to take a quick photo.

Great, so as you see, we're really trying to make up for on the timing, so apologies if we're running a bit. But Julia and I have the task and the privilege to share with you a little bit of the background of where we are now, as well as where we're trying to go, and the process in the next two and a half days, let's say. So as Frida mentioned in her remarks this morning, the road map that we're developing is really a very consultative process in which we're really trying to engage as many actors and partners, but also ensure that everything we do is linked to existing strategies, policies, commitments that already exist.

Again, we're not trying to reinvent the wheel, but we're trying to make sure that we have something really specific and clear on midwifery for the continent from the continent. So what we've done so far to get to this point today is to go through a consultative process. So you'll see, yeah, it's a bit, one more, yeah, there you go.

So on step one, how we got here, we have reviewed more than 25 global, continental, and sub-regional documents on midwifery in Africa. Okay, so again, we tried to look at what's out there, what already exists. Then we called for three sub-regional consultations, one for North Africa and a few of the Horn of Africa countries, right, from that North Africa region that I just explained, one for West and Central Africa, and one from East and Southern Africa.

Those were virtual, they were online consultations where we went through and had discussions and some small group work exercises to try to elicit challenges and priorities that were affecting those specific sub-regions. And you can see on the right, we have a breakdown as well of how many participants and how many organizations were involved in each of those. So if I do the quick math, because I didn't think of this ahead, it looks like it's over 130 participants and what, 27, 33 or 34 organizations.

So it really was a very consultative process and we thank all of you who were able to contribute to those. Following that desk review and the consultations, the virtual consultations, then there was a synthesis that was undertaken, right. So we had a team of consultants working with the UNFP team and colleagues also from JAPAEGO to try to go through all of the rich information recommendations that came out of those consultations to really hone in on what are some of the key actions that the participants felt could make a difference, could really accelerate midwifery across the African continent.

So what we've come up with and what's available now is for each accelerator, we have a list of eight, between eight and ten actions that were identified through that consultative process. And today, starting after lunch, and Julie will explain and go through the process in detail, we're now going to step four, where we're using your expertise and your ambitions really to help us to hone in. So again, where we have 10 activities per accelerator, we want to try to get that list down to five activities per accelerator.
